doc: THE list of atom types. Labelers, the type heads' label space, the facet map and the prod enum are all checked against this file (tests/test_atom_type_registry.py). To add a type: add it here with status 'v2', then follow the test failures.

keep.name: _keep
keep.desc: Noise: a line with no fact for anyone. Greetings and closers are small talk; this is the rest: message headers and wrappers, legal and confidentiality footers, page chrome, empty cells and value-less column labels, template instructions, a broad heading with no list under it, a sentence that only points at another clause or an attachment. A signature line names a person and is a stakeholder; a heading over a list is a list header.

context_hints.label: The words themselves
context_hints.desc: The line's own words decided it; nothing around it was needed.

context_hints.label: Section heading
context_hints.desc: The heading of the section the line sits in decided it.

context_hints.label: Intro line above a list
context_hints.desc: The intro line above a list ("Provided by the customer:") decided it.

context_hints.label: Atom above
context_hints.desc: The line just above decided it.

context_hints.label: Atom below
context_hints.desc: The line just below decided it.

context_hints.label: Who said it, and to whom
context_hints.desc: Who wrote or said it, and to whom, decided it.

context_hints.label: Table column / header row
context_hints.desc: The table column or header row it sits under decided it.

context_hints.label: What kind of document
context_hints.desc: The kind of document (email, SOW, BOM, call note) decided it.

context_hints.label: Another document in the deal
context_hints.desc: Another document in the deal decided it.

context_hints.label: Industry knowledge
context_hints.desc: Trade knowledge decided it: what any installer would know about the work.

types.name: physical_site
types.desc: A place the work happens at or is about, named in any form: a street address, a store or building name with a number, a campus, or only a town and state. One learned line per place; other mentions are copies. A removed site stays a site line, marked superseded. Unlike a site attribute (a count or size about the place), a site implementation note (what to install there or how) or a stakeholder (the person at the place).

types.name: site_attribute
types.desc: A number or property of one site: users, rooms, phones, floors, buildings, square feet, priority. Unlike a site line it does not name the place; unlike a quantity it belongs to a named site.

types.name: site_access_restriction
types.desc: A constraint on access: blackout window, restricted hours, badged escort required, weekend-only cutover, etc.

types.name: site_room_mix
types.desc: A row from a per-site room-mix table: room type + count + standard build + validation test.

types.name: site_infrastructure
types.desc: Site-bound infrastructure facts: MDF/IDF id, bandwidth/circuit, cable plant condition.

types.name: derived_finding
types.desc: A statement nobody wrote: counted, measured or noticed-to-be-absent by the parser from an artifact's own structure -- 106 workstations counted as CAD block inserts, 828 ft of new partition summed from linework, a telecom layer noticed missing. Carries what it assumed and what it decides, because a derived claim has to be arguable.

types.name: deal_state
types.desc: Where the deal stands, derived from its own sentences rather than written by anyone: the step it waits on, who owns that step, and whether its price has been checked against the site. Consolidates the coordination traffic -- scheduling, acknowledgements, chasing -- that moves a deal but never reaches a SOW.

types.name: service_line
types.desc: A priced service with a quantity and a rate, in any form: "Technician per day, 4 locations x 52 days, $920, $191,360".

types.name: bom_line
types.desc: A material or part with a quantity, and often a model or price: "12 x outdoor access point".

types.name: payment_term
types.desc: When and how invoices are raised and paid: monthly in arrears, a deposit and a balance, net 30, remit-to details.

types.name: commercial_total
types.desc: An aggregate price line: hardware subtotal, services subtotal, freight/logistics, contingency, taxes, grand total. Each is one atom.

types.name: pricing_assumption
types.desc: A term that sets how the price is worked out: billing basis (time and materials), billing increments, minimums, the standard day, after-hours or weekend rates, "merely an estimate", quote validity, taxes. Invoice timing is a payment term; cancellation charges are a change-order rule.

types.name: site_budget
types.desc: Per-site budget category amount (hardware budget / services budget / logistics estimate per site).

types.name: rate_card
types.desc: A rate for a role or service with no quantity: a bill rate, overtime or holiday multiplier, minimum hours.

types.name: work_scope_item
types.desc: A service the customer is buying, said at the level of the service, not one step: a recurring visit and its hours, on-call coverage, end-user support, the broad first line that names a support area, one site's row in a per-site scope grid, or a side remark that opens new work.

types.name: deal_summary
types.desc: The one line the whole deal can be read from: the service-model or job overview sentence ("4 TVs install in the New York office"). At most one per deal; a scope opener that restates one line is not it.

types.name: requirement
types.desc: A formally numbered requirement (REQ-001 style) with applies-to + owner + verification method.

types.name: task
types.desc: One step of work someone performs, with an owner: the provider's billable work ("install three cameras at the side, back and front doors", "relocate 10 access points", "perform basic network validation"), or a step the provider's seller, architect or coordinator takes ("let me get this in front of my architect"; those are the seller's own steps, not priced work). Unlike a work scope item, it is one step, not the service bought. Unlike a dependency, the provider does it, not the customer. Unlike a commitment, it names no promise to the other party by a date. Unlike a deliverable, nothing is handed over.

types.name: deliverable
types.desc: Something handed over when the work is done: a report, as-built drawings, test results, completion status, documentation.

types.name: acceptance_criterion
types.desc: A row from an acceptance-criteria table — area + criteria + pass threshold.

types.name: milestone_phase
types.desc: A row from a project phase/milestone table — phase number + name + start date + end date + owner + exit criteria. Synonyms accepted: phase, sprint, wave, milestone, stage.

types.name: cutover_step
types.desc: A row from a cutover/runbook checklist — step number + timing relative to cutover + owner + action + evidence required.

types.name: electrical_acceptance_test
types.desc: A measurable electrical/network acceptance test (Megger, ground resistance, load burn-in, witness/ATP).

types.name: site_implementation_note
types.desc: How or with what the work is done at one site: the equipment there and its models, where a cable lands, a receiving or install rule, an asset-tag prefix. Unlike a constraint, it describes the build, not a limit on when or how.

types.name: site_access_window
types.desc: When a site is accessible — days + hours + escort owner.

types.name: exclusion
types.desc: Work or items the job explicitly leaves out, from either side: "electrical by others", "we don't provide parts", "remote support not included".

types.name: integration_checkpoint
types.desc: A row from a system-to-system integration checkpoint table: checkpoint id + system + expected input/output + owner + due.

types.name: data_flow_step
types.desc: One step of a data-flow pipeline (source system → sink system, what payload).

types.name: system_mapping
types.desc: A field mapping between two systems: which field in one fills which field in the other.

types.name: mitigation
types.desc: A mitigation paired with a specific risk (separate from the risk atom itself).

types.name: constraint
types.desc: A limit on how, when or where the provider may work: hours, noise, dust, union labour, escalate only when approved, ports to leave unused. Unlike an exclusion, the work is still in scope.

types.name: compliance_rule
types.desc: A rule about access, data handling, retention, credential use, or auditing.

types.name: compliance_classification
types.desc: A document/data classification + its allowed and blocked destinations (Confidential, Internal, Mock, Production).

types.name: approval_authority
types.desc: A rule that some role/threshold requires a specific approver (e.g. 'CFO signoff required over $1.5M').

types.name: submission_req
types.desc: A required element of the proposal submission: number of copies, file format, required form (SF330, W-9), page limit, sealed-bid labeling, delivery method.

types.name: change_order_rule
types.desc: A rule that governs change orders — when one is required, T&M rate caps, materials markup, the rate for change-order work. A standing rate term (after-hours billed at 150%) is a pricing_assumption.

types.name: bonding_insurance
types.desc: A bonding or insurance requirement: bid bond, performance bond, payment bond, general liability limit, workers comp, professional liability.

types.name: contract_term
types.desc: A legal term of the agreement: length and renewal, warranty, liability, rate adjustments, fee definitions, acceptance by signature, termination. Payment timing is a payment term.

types.name: certification
types.desc: A certification or credential the provider or its technicians must hold (e.g. BICSI RCDD, OSHA-10, manufacturer cert).

types.name: stakeholder
types.desc: A line that names a person: an email signature (name, title, phone, email), an introduction or CC ("looping in Sean"), a contact-table row, a requester cell, a site contact with a role. It says who the person is and whose side they are on, not what the job is. Unlike a signatory, nobody signs here; unlike an entity, the name is a person.

types.name: blackout_date_range
types.desc: A no-work date window (holiday freeze, exec blackout, peak travel exclusion).

types.name: lead_time_constraint
types.desc: Lead time + expediting policy for an item class (core switches, APs, AV kits, fiber panels, custom millwork).

types.name: deadline
types.desc: A hard date/time the bidder must meet: proposal/bid due date, questions-due date, pre-bid meeting, site visit. NOT a project phase end (that is milestone_phase).

types.name: dependency
types.desc: Something the customer or a third party must do or supply before the work can go ahead: send floor plans, provide access or a reachable contact, have equipment on site. If the provider did it, it would be a task.

types.name: deal_metadata
types.desc: Header-level fact about the deal itself: customer name, deal ID, quote/PO/MSA references, contract type, currency, target close date, deal stage.

types.name: source_caveat
types.desc: A fact about a document that changes how it must be read: it is a draft, it is not a contract, part of it is wrong, something supersedes it. Never scope; it travels with the document it is about.

types.name: legend_entry
types.desc: The key to a drawing or sheet: what a colour, symbol, hatch or abbreviation means there ("hatched = by others"). Not scope; it exists so a correction can point at it. Unlike a source caveat, it is the thing corrected, not the correction.

types.name: list_header
types.desc: A heading or lead-in that only points at the lines under it ("Locations:", "The following items are excluded:"). Background, not an input: its meaning lives in the items it governs.

types.name: eval_criterion
types.desc: A scored evaluation/award criterion with its weight: 'Technical approach 40%', 'Price 30%', 'Past performance 20%'. One per criterion.

types.name: approval_decision
types.desc: A recorded approval/conditional approval/rejection statement by a named stakeholder.

types.name: metadata_requirement
types.desc: A required metadata key/value to set on an object (blob metadata, CRM custom field).

types.name: signatory
types.desc: A signature-block entry — role + named person who signs.

types.name: addendum_qa
types.desc: An addendum, amendment, or question-and-answer item issued during the solicitation that modifies or clarifies the original documents.

types.name: site_allocation
types.desc: Per-site qty breakdown of a single BOM line (e.g. 'HW-001: ATL-HQ:52; ATL-WEST:27; ATL-AIR:15').

types.name: scope_item
types.desc: Legacy catch-all for a line of scope. Prefer a finer type; use only when none fits.

types.name: risk
types.desc: A stated risk or concern that could affect delivery, cost or schedule.

types.name: assumption
types.desc: A condition of the site or job the price and plan take to be true, which if false changes them: "pathways exist", "existing cable is reusable". Unlike a dependency, nobody is asked to do anything; unlike a pricing assumption, it is about the site or work, not the price terms.

types.name: open_question
types.desc: A question or an unknown left unanswered in the deal ("no idea of ticket volume yet"), which someone must resolve.

types.name: decision
types.desc: A decision already made and recorded ("customer chose option B").

types.name: action_item
types.desc: A to-do assigned to a named person, without a price or a promise to the other party: "Mark to send the floor plan".

types.name: vendor_line_item
types.desc: A vendor quote/BOM line: part, quantity, price.

types.name: customer_instruction
types.desc: A direct instruction from the customer about how to do the work.

types.name: quantity
types.desc: A bare count of a thing ("110 TVs", "24 drops") not attached to a line item.

types.name: entity
types.desc: A named thing (company, product, person) with no claim attached.

types.name: answered_question
types.desc: A question that a later line answers, or a note that two documents disagree that a later line settles. The answer is its own line and links back with answers.

types.name: internal_question
types.desc: A question between people on our own team (routing, who to ask, pricing among ourselves). Never a question for the customer.

types.name: commitment
types.desc: A promise to act made to the other party: "we will send the floor plan Friday", an assurance the provider can support the sites, an offered call time. Unlike a task, the promise itself is the fact.

types.name: small_talk
types.desc: Relationship talk that carries no fact about the work: thanks, greetings, banter, "sending this to my team". If the line ALSO says something about the job (its size, a document we need, a promise), it is not small talk.

service_packs_doc: Deal-level router gold: the labeler's answer to 'what is this deal mainly?'. Ids match Orbitbrief-Core world_model/data/domain_packs.yaml.

suppliers.label: The provider
suppliers.desc: The provider that wrote the quote does or supplies it: its work, steps, terms, prices, exclusions and risks, and a customer's ask for work the provider would do.

suppliers.label: Partner / reseller
suppliers.desc: The reseller or channel partner between provider and customer does or supplies it: its paperwork, its practice, its own chasing, a line naming the partner company.

suppliers.label: End customer
suppliers.desc: The end customer does, supplies or owns it: its sites, its decisions, its equipment, the inputs it owes before work can go ahead, its own situation.

suppliers.label: Another party
suppliers.desc: Someone outside provider, partner and customer: another contractor, a manufacturer or vendor, a carrier, a landlord, an inspector.

suppliers.label: Not settled
suppliers.desc: The deal does not say who: a question that names nobody to answer it, or a role that could be either side ("provided by installer"). Usually an unpriced cost.

suppliers_doc: Who supplies, does or owns what the line states. The provider is the company that wrote the quote; the customer is the end customer whose site it is; a partner is the reseller between them; a third party is anyone else (another contractor, a manufacturer, a carrier, a landlord). A person's line takes the side of the person's employer. A status report takes the side whose progress it reports. A question takes unresolved unless it names who must answer. An answer takes the party whose fact it is. Headings, totals, noise and lines with no party take none.
about_doc: Whose fact is it? The type says what a line is; this says what it is about. deal: this job. account: the customer relationship beyond this job. partner: how the reseller works. internal: how the provider itself works. A person's contact or signature line is about the side the person works for (provider staff internal, partner staff partner, customer staff account) unless it gives the person's role on this job (site contact, requester, contact table), which makes it deal.

about.label: This job
about.desc: This job's scope, sites, price, schedule or people in their role on it.

about.label: The customer relationship
about.desc: True of the customer beyond this job: who decides, how they buy, room to grow, their own staff and process.

about.label: The partner's way of working
about.desc: How the reseller works: its paperwork, approvals, chasing and its own staff.

about.label: The provider's own process
about.desc: How the provider works inside: its routing, its own staff and its own bookkeeping. Never a deliverable.

wants_doc: What the line asks someone to do before the job can be priced or run. Most lines want nothing. A line wants something only when it leaves a gap open: a document named but not held, a conversation referred to but not in the deal, a question for the customer, or a choice the provider must make.

wants.label: Nothing
wants.desc: The line is simply true or settled; nobody has to fetch, ask or decide anything.

wants.label: Get a document
wants.desc: It names a drawing, floor plan, photo, quote or report the deal does not hold.

wants.label: Find the conversation
wants.desc: It refers to a call, meeting or thread the deal does not hold ("as discussed").

wants.label: Ask the customer
wants.desc: An open question only the customer can answer, and the price, scope or schedule waits on it.

wants.label: The provider decides
wants.desc: Only the provider can settle it: a staffing, method or pricing choice of its own.

reads_doc: What an atom TELLS US. Each key is a learned head: a rule fills it today as a prediction (source=rule, low confidence) purely so a labeler has something to confirm or drop, and the confirmations train the head that replaces the rule. A keyword list cannot make these calls -- it hid a promise naming a deal's decision maker because the words looked like banter. See _LABELING_DOCTRINE.md. `layer` says who a reading is true for. universal: any field-services company reading the same line would give the same answer; the base model trains it. company: the answer depends on our business model, roles, pricing, product names or CRM; only that company's profile trains it, and its keys start co_ when new. meta: stored on the row for bookkeeping (whose policy, how the deal ended) and never a task or a model input. staging: a temporary key a backfill uses, never a task. A labeling page shows universal and company chips only. `multi: true` means the value is a list, one class per item. `value_desc` gives every answer of a closed list its written description. The heads are built from these words (a question's description, then each answer's), so they say what the answer means for any company and name no company's tools; a company reading may name ours.

reads.label: Just relationship talk
reads.desc: Thanks, greetings, banter. NOT small talk if it also says anything about the work, promises something, or names a person or a document.

reads.label: How big the sender thinks it is
reads.desc: Sizing in the sender's own words, before any site visit.

value_desc.small: The sender calls the job small, quick or simple, or sizes it at a handful of devices, rooms or hours, before anyone has walked the site.
value_desc.large: The sender calls the job large, a full build-out or a multi-phase project, or sizes it at many sites, floors or days, before anyone has walked the site.

reads.label: Display size
reads.desc: The screen size the line states: "75 inch" is 75. Size sets how many techs a mount takes.

reads.label: How many units
reads.desc: The count of displays, devices or units the line states. A count of sites is job_scale; a count of people is crew_size.

reads.label: What kind of requirement
reads.values: access | schedule | personnel | safety | access_equipment | tech_toolkit | technical_spec | documentation | commercial
reads.desc: The kind of requirement the line states: getting in, timing, who the workers must be, safety, equipment to reach the work, the tools a technician brings, how the work must be built, documents to produce or hand over, or contract terms. A line that names several takes the one it leads with or spends the most words on.

value_desc.access: Getting in to do the work, physical or logical: badges, escorts, check-in, parking or dock, permits and landlord approvals, access hours, credentials, admin rights and logins.
value_desc.schedule: When the work may happen or how much notice it needs: work windows, after-hours or weekend-only work, blackout days, notice periods and lead days before scheduling.
value_desc.personnel: Who the workers must be: background checks, drug screens, identity or citizenship vetting, licenses or certifications, union or prevailing-wage labor, required roles, skills and crew make-up.
value_desc.safety: Safety rules and protective gear: PPE, site safety plans, lockout/tagout, confined-space programs, spotters and harnesses, and hazard procedures.
value_desc.access_equipment: Equipment needed to reach the work: ladders, scissor, boom or server lifts, scaffolds, telehandlers and bucket trucks.
value_desc.tech_toolkit: Tools and devices the technician brings and takes away again: hand and power tools, testers, toners, crimpers, label makers, laptops and console cables.
value_desc.technical_spec: How the work or the site must be built or configured: standards, cable and fiber types, termination and labeling rules, hardware or material to install, and technical preconditions such as power or network in place.
value_desc.documentation: Documents to produce or hand over: as-builts, completion photos, test reports, closeout packages, and customer-supplied runbooks, designs or floor plans.
value_desc.commercial: Contract and business terms: insurance and certificates of insurance, bonds, purchase orders, tax certificates, proposal format, confidentiality, and business certifications.

reads.label: Material named
reads.desc: A material or consumable the line names (cable, mounts, conduit), in its own words.

reads.label: Whose side of the scope
reads.desc: Who the line puts the work or item on: the provider doing the job, the customer, a third party, or both.

value_desc.provider: The service provider doing the job does the work or brings the item.
value_desc.customer: The end customer does the work or supplies the item themselves.
value_desc.third_party: Someone outside the provider and the customer does it, such as another contractor, the landlord, a carrier or a manufacturer.
value_desc.shared: Two or more parties split it, and the line says or implies each side's part.

reads.label: Which site
reads.desc: The site the line is about, by the name the text uses.

reads.label: Where it is
reads.desc: The address or place the line gives, verbatim.

reads.label: A rate the line states
reads.desc: A price per unit of work the text gives ("$95/hr", "$920 per day"). Whether it is our rate or theirs is policy, not this reading.

reads.label: What the rate is for
reads.desc: The work or role the stated rate applies to ("lead tech", "after-hours").

reads.label: Room to grow on this account
reads.desc: This job could repeat across more of the customer's sites. Say WHAT repeats ("more clubs, same one-door scope"), not just that it might. Never scope; it belongs in the brief's why-you-should-care, and it is why a small job can be worth quoting keenly.

reads.label: Somebody undertook to do something
reads.desc: A promise with an owner. A promise conditional on OUR answer is a task on us before it is one on them.

reads.label: Brings in someone not in this thread
reads.values: the role, and the name when we have one
reads.desc: A decision maker, landlord, installer or facilities manager being brought into the deal. Write the role alone when nobody named them ("club owner") -- that absence IS the finding, because we cannot contact a role.

reads.label: Points at something we do not hold
reads.desc: A call or a file the deal does not contain, which someone would have to go and get.

value_desc.conversation: The line refers to a call, meeting or message thread the deal does not contain ("as discussed", "per our call").
value_desc.attachment: The line refers to a file the deal does not contain: a drawing, photo, quote, spreadsheet or signed form.

reads.label: A document to go and get
reads.desc: A drawing, floorplan or spec the sender names and the deal does not hold.

reads.label: Names a document
reads.desc: The line refers to a drawing or file, whether or not we hold it.

reads.label: It cannot happen until somebody answers
reads.desc: The line is conditional: "if you all would be able to…, I will…". Whoever must answer owns the deal's next move, and a promise waiting on the provider is a task on the provider before it is one on anyone else. This is the critical path, and it is invisible if the conditional is flattened into the type.

value_desc.us: The service provider writing or receiving the quote must answer or act first; the line waits on the provider's own side.
value_desc.customer: The end customer must answer, approve or provide something first.
value_desc.partner: A reseller, vendor or other contractor must answer or act first.

reads.label: It announces what follows
reads.desc: "Here are the details for the small job" governs everything under it until the next announcement. The atoms below inherit its readings -- job_scale applies to THOSE ten items, not to the whole thread. Which atoms it covers is the `governs` link, not this reading.

reads.label: It only introduces a list
reads.desc: The line only announces the list under it ("The following sites are included:"). It governs each item.

reads.label: How many lines it governs
reads.desc: How many lines the header or summary governs. Bookkeeping for the governs links.

reads.label: How many lines it was derived from
reads.desc: Bookkeeping for the derived_from links.

reads.label: Which part of it must not be trusted
reads.values: the part, in the document's own words
reads.desc: Name the section, legend or column that is wrong -- "Installer Supplied Components" -- not just that something is. This is the reading that has to be carried down into the analysis of the document: a caveat nobody can act on is a caveat nobody applies.

reads.label: Matters here, generalises nowhere
reads.values: what it is doing on this deal
reads.desc: Worth keeping for anyone reading THIS deal and worth no rule at all. Not a fact about the work, not pure boilerplate: the acknowledgement that explains why a second message arrived, the forward that says who now holds the job, the aside that only means something next to the line above it. Say what it is doing HERE -- "explains why the address came separately" -- never just that it is minor. `_keep` deletes a line; this one preserves it without teaching anything, which is the whole difference. A head should come away from it with nothing.

reads.label: The deal's scope in one line
reads.desc: THE line a router should read the whole deal from: service, quantity, site and deal type in one sentence -- "4 TVs install in CheckOut New York office." At most one per deal: if you mark a second line, training keeps only your latest mark. Every other line you labeled on that deal teaches "not the summary". Not every scope line -- a work_scope_item says one thing the job includes; this says what the job IS.

reads.label: Takes a cost off our quote
reads.values: which cost, and why it goes
reads.desc: Somebody else covers something we would otherwise price: "the customer provides the wall mounts and parking" removes the wall-mount and parking costs. Name WHICH cost goes, in the line's own words, not just that one does. Link the line to the quote, schedule or BOM row it removes; if that row still charges for it, that is a Conflict.

reads.label: How urgent it is
reads.values: how soon, and what drives it
reads.desc: A deadline, rush or priority signal: "need this installed before the store opens on the 15th", "ASAP, customer is escalating". Say how soon and why, in the line's own words. A date that is only a schedule fact with no pressure behind it is not urgency.

reads.label: A task that starts when something happens
reads.desc: A PM, PC, SA or tech will act once an event lands: "as soon as we receive confirmation that the TVs have arrived on site, we will coordinate a date". Name the event in the line's own words ("TVs confirmed on site"). Link the event's atom with triggered_by when it arrives, the dependency with blocked_by, and the task with context. A seller saying they will reply or send something is not a task for us.

reads.label: Whose task it is
reads.values: project_manager | project_coordinator | solutions_architect | technician | seller | customer | partner | other
reads.desc: Who owns the step or task the line states or starts. Delivery roles: project manager, project coordinator, solutions architect, technician. A step the provider's seller takes (taking a request to an architect, offering call times) is seller. Steps the customer, the partner or anyone else owns take their side. Put the named person in entity_keys.

value_desc.project_manager: The project manager who runs the job day to day: schedule, budget and customer updates.
value_desc.project_coordinator: The coordinator who books visits, ships equipment and keeps the paperwork moving.
value_desc.solutions_architect: The technical designer who scopes the system, draws it and answers how it should be built.
value_desc.technician: The technician on site who installs, tests and documents the work.
value_desc.seller: The provider's salesperson or account manager owns the step: a sales follow-up, sending a quote, offering call times. It is a step, not work the quote prices.
value_desc.customer: Someone on the customer's side owns the task.
value_desc.partner: The reseller or channel partner owns the task.
value_desc.other: Someone outside the provider, partner and customer owns it: another contractor, a manufacturer, a landlord, an inspector.

reads.label: How many people go
reads.desc: The number of techs or crew sent or planned for the job: "Tanner chose to send 2 techs out" is 2. A count of devices or sites is job_scale, not crew size.

reads.label: Tech skill level
reads.values: the level the text asks for
reads.desc: The skill level or certification the work needs, in the text's own words.

reads.label: Which techs cover it
reads.desc: Which techs, pool or area covers the work ("local tech", "travel from Dallas").

reads.label: Labor hours the line states
reads.desc: The labor hours the text gives. hours_stated says whether there are any; this is the number. Our own estimate is co_hours_estimate.

reads.label: How often
reads.desc: How often the work recurs ("monthly", "2 visits per quarter").

reads.label: Lead time
reads.desc: How long before the work something must happen or arrive ("2 weeks notice", "6-8 week lead on displays").

reads.label: A template placeholder
reads.desc: The line is an unfilled template slot ("[Customer Name]", "TBD") rather than a fact.

reads.label: An event that starts a task
reads.desc: The line only reports that something happened, and that happening starts a waiting task: "TVs were delivered today". It is not scope and adds no work of its own, so planning and runbooks skip it. Link the task's atom to it with triggered_by.

reads.label: Which task it starts
reads.desc: The task this event starts, in short words: "PM schedules the install date with the customer". Pairs with trigger_event.

reads.label: Where the deal was when this was said
reads.desc: The coarse stage when this source entered the deal (from its arrival date, not a date inside it): quoting runs until the statement of work is signed or the order arrives; planning until the first visit; delivery while visits run; closeout after the last.

value_desc.quoting: Before the SOW is signed or the purchase order is received; the price is still being worked out.
value_desc.planning: After the purchase order, before the first visit on site; dates, crews and equipment are being lined up.
value_desc.delivery: Visits are underway; work is being done on site.
value_desc.closeout: After the last visit: completion reports, sign-off, invoicing and punch-list follow-up.

reads.label: When the work starts
reads.values: the confirmed or proposed start date/time
reads.desc: The line sets or proposes when on-site work begins: "see you Friday at 9am". Copy the date and time as said. Label the confirmed start once, on the line that confirms it; an earlier proposal that changed is superseded by it.

reads.label: How the work is billed
reads.desc: The pricing basis a line states: one fixed price, time and materials (units times a rate, so every total is an estimate), milestone payments, or a price per site (a unit times the site count). Same values as the deal-level billing judgment.

value_desc.fixed: One fixed price for the stated scope, whatever the hours turn out to be.
value_desc.t_and_m: Time and materials: hours or units times a rate, so any total is an estimate.
value_desc.milestone: Payments tied to stages of the work, such as a deposit, a mid-point payment and a payment on completion.
value_desc.per_site: A price per site, multiplied by the number of sites.

reads.label: Should have been asked at quoting
reads.desc: A planning or delivery question about a site or customer fact that intake should have collected before the quote: "is there power at the TV location?" asked after the PO. Orbit learns to ask it earlier.

reads.label: Who needs the answer
reads.values: project_manager | atlas | portal | quoting | sow | delivery
reads.desc: Who downstream needs this fact: the PM running the job, Atlas planning, the customer portal, quoting (the quote and the Deal Kit), the SOW, or delivery (dispatch and the techs on site). A list; a fact can feed several.

value_desc.project_manager: The project manager running the job needs it to plan or run the work.
value_desc.atlas: Our Atlas planning tool needs it to build the plan and schedule.
value_desc.portal: The customer portal needs it, so the customer can see it.
value_desc.quoting: Quoting needs it: the quote and the Deal Kit that prices it.
value_desc.sow: The SOW needs it: it belongs in the written scope.
value_desc.delivery: Delivery needs it: dispatch and the techs on site.

reads.label: Which parser learns from it
reads.desc: The consumer this line trains: quote_parser reads a deal before the quote, delivery_parser reads what governs the work after it is sold. A list; a line can feed both.

value_desc.quote_parser: The line matters before the sale: it helps read a deal well enough to price it.
value_desc.delivery_parser: The line matters after the sale: it governs how the sold work is carried out.

reads.label: Filled in or still the template
reads.desc: Is the statement-of-work line written for this deal or the provider's standing wording? Judge it across the provider's SOWs: the same wording appears in other SOWs from the same provider when it is template. A template clause that sets a real term here, including a condition that could bite (an after-hours uplift, a minimum, billing in arrears), is template_applies and is a learned line; template wording that sets nothing on this job is background. This is about the wording; how a value was reached is the derivation reading.

value_desc.filled: Written for this deal: its names, counts, dates, sites or steps.
value_desc.template: The provider's standing wording or an unfilled placeholder that sets nothing on this job: background.
value_desc.template_applies: The provider's standing wording that still sets a term this job follows or could trigger: a rate uplift, minimum, cancellation fee, billing timing, quote validity.

reads.label: How the SOW covers it
reads.desc: How the final statement of work treats the fact. On a request line (an ask): in_sow if the SOW carries it unchanged, differs if the SOW carries it with another number, site, date or party, missing_from_sow if it never arrived. On a SOW line: in_sow or differs when an earlier ask lies behind it, sow_only when no customer or partner asked and the provider's own document is the first to offer it. sow_not_available when the deal holds no SOW. Sites always carry coverage. Copies, pointers, contact and signature rows, chatter and status lines take none.

value_desc.in_sow: The SOW states the same fact, possibly in other words.
value_desc.missing_from_sow: The fact is real and affects the work, but the SOW never states it.
value_desc.differs: The SOW states the same fact with another value; the line that states the changed value carries it, and rows computed from the agreed values do not.
value_desc.sow_not_available: The deal holds no SOW to check against yet.
value_desc.sow_only: No customer or partner asked for it; the provider's own SOW (or its own earlier quote) is where it first appears: template terms, rates, house clauses.

reads.label: Why the SOW covers it that way
reads.desc: The reasoning behind sow_coverage on this line, in a sentence.

reads.label: Which SOW section it belongs in
reads.values: overview | scope_of_work | deliverables | acceptance | out_of_scope | assumptions | customer_responsibilities | provider_responsibilities | timeline | fees | change_control | terms | contacts | other
reads.desc: The standard section of a statement of work this line belongs in, judged by what the line does, not by the words of the heading it sits under: a heading named 'Scope of Services' or 'Project Scope' is scope_of_work; 'Pricing and Invoice Schedule', 'Billing Terms', 'Travel' and 'Expenses' are fees; 'Duration' and 'Project Scheduling' are timeline; 'Contact Information' and 'Team' are contacts; a per-site exhibit row is scope_of_work. provider_responsibilities is the provider's side and customer_responsibilities the customer's, whatever the document calls them. Lines that are not in a statement of work take the section they would land in.

value_desc.overview: The introduction, executive summary or project overview: what the project is and why.
value_desc.scope_of_work: The work to be done: tasks, quantities and where.
value_desc.deliverables: What is handed over at the end: equipment in place, documents, drawings or test results.
value_desc.acceptance: How the work is accepted as complete: the criteria, tests or sign-off.
value_desc.out_of_scope: What the job explicitly does not include.
value_desc.assumptions: What the price and plan assume to be true, such as access, existing conditions or working hours.
value_desc.customer_responsibilities: What the customer must do or provide.
value_desc.provider_responsibilities: What the service provider must do or provide beyond the listed tasks.
value_desc.timeline: Dates, durations, phases and the order of the work.
value_desc.fees: Prices, rates, payment terms and invoicing.
value_desc.change_control: How changes to the scope are requested, priced and approved.
value_desc.terms: Termination and the other legal terms: liability, warranty, governing law.
value_desc.contacts: Who the people are and how to reach them.
value_desc.other: A real SOW line that fits none of the sections above.

reads.label: How the value was arrived at
reads.desc: stated: the text says it. inferred: it follows from the text and trade knowledge. template: it came from a template default. not_derivable: nothing on the page supports it.

value_desc.stated: The text says the value outright.
value_desc.inferred: The value follows from the text plus trade knowledge, but the text does not say it.
value_desc.template: The value came from a template default, not from this deal.
value_desc.not_derivable: Nothing on the page supports the value.

reads.label: Why the value was arrived at that way
reads.desc: The reasoning behind derivation on this line, in a sentence.

reads.label: A SOW existed when this was written
reads.desc: Whether the deal held a SOW at the time of this line, so coverage is judged against what existed then.

reads.label: Why a SOW did or did not exist then
reads.desc: The reasoning behind sow_available_at_stage on this line, in a sentence.

reads.label: What labor market the site is in
reads.desc: Geography only: whether a metro tech pool is within reach of the site. How a company prices a tier is its own policy and is not labeled here. A list only on a line that covers several sites, one tier per site; a single site has one tier.

value_desc.major_metro: Inside or next to a large metropolitan area, where many technicians live.
value_desc.mid_metro: In or near a mid-sized metro area with a smaller technician pool.
value_desc.small_town: A small town some distance from a metro area; technicians have to travel.
value_desc.rural: Rural, far from any metro area; travel, lodging or a long drive is likely.

reads.label: Region
reads.desc: The metro area, region or state the line places the work in.

reads.label: How precise the address is
reads.values: full | street_no_zip | street_no_city | street_only | city_only | region_only | state_only | name_only
reads.desc: full: a street address with city and zip. street_no_zip: street and city, no zip. street_no_city: a street and number but no city. street_only: a street name with no number or city. city_only: only a city. region_only: only a metro area or region ("Chicago area"). state_only: only a state. name_only: only a site or building name.

value_desc.full: A complete street address with number, street, city and zip.
value_desc.street_no_zip: A street address and city, but the zip code is missing.
value_desc.street_no_city: A street and number, but neither the city nor the zip.
value_desc.street_only: Only a street name, with no house number and no city.
value_desc.city_only: Only a city is named, with no street.
value_desc.region_only: Only a metro area or region is named ("Chicago area").
value_desc.state_only: Only a state is named, with no city.
value_desc.name_only: Only a site or building name, with no address at all.

reads.label: What the address is missing
reads.desc: The reasoning behind address_level on this line, in a sentence.

reads.label: How far from the nearest metro
reads.values: the distance, as written or measured
reads.desc: Distance from the site to the nearest metro area above a set size, e.g. "85 miles from Denver". Never distance from a company's own techs or offices.

reads.label: What kind of document it comes from
reads.desc: The document's own kind (quote, BOM, SOW, floor plan, email), beyond the file type.

reads.label: What the cell is in a BOM row
reads.desc: The role of this value in its bill-of-materials row: part number, description, quantity, unit_price, ext_price, and so on.

reads.label: Canonical deal stage when written
reads.values: pre_deal | intake | scoping | quoted | contracting | planning | delivery | closeout | unknown
reads.desc: The stage of the deal when this source entered it: its arrival date against the deal's milestones, never a date printed inside it. Every line of one message or document takes the same stage.

value_desc.pre_deal: Before there is a deal: an intro, a relationship note or a general inquiry.
value_desc.intake: The request has just arrived: first details, sites and contacts, before any walkthrough or price.
value_desc.scoping: The work is being defined before a price: walkthroughs, questions, drawings, site lists.
value_desc.quoted: A price has been sent and the deal waits on a decision; no statement of work is out yet.
value_desc.contracting: A statement-of-work draft or contract is out for review or signature.
value_desc.planning: Signed or ordered, before the first visit: scheduling, staffing, shipping.
value_desc.closeout: The work is done: sign-off, reports, invoicing and punch list.
value_desc.unknown: The line does not show which stage the deal was in.

reads.label: What kind of scope line
reads.values: summary | work_step | schedule | tooling | materials | staffing | testing | documentation | responsibility | exclusion | other
reads.desc: The kind of scope line, the same for any provider. Set it on learned scope lines only, never on copies. A customer duty or dependency is responsibility; an exclusion is exclusion.

value_desc.summary: Says what the whole job or a whole phase is, in one line.
value_desc.work_step: One step the crew performs: mount, run, terminate, configure, test-and-hand-over of one item.
value_desc.schedule: When the work happens, how often, or how long it takes: dates, windows, cadence.
value_desc.tooling: Tools, lifts or equipment the crew needs to do the work.
value_desc.materials: The parts and materials installed or consumed.
value_desc.staffing: How many people, which skills or how many visits.
value_desc.testing: Tests, certification or verification of the work.
value_desc.documentation: Drawings, as-builts, photos, reports or labels handed over.
value_desc.responsibility: What one side owes the other: a customer input or duty, or a split of duties.
value_desc.other: A scope line none of the kinds above fits.

reads.label: What kind of noise
reads.values: greeting_thanks | banter_reassurance | signoff_wrapper | legal_footer | automated_wrapper | table_scaffolding | section_heading | attachment_pointer | speech_filler | page_chrome | template_instruction | cross_reference
reads.desc: Only on _keep and small_talk rows: which kind of line carries no fact for anyone.

value_desc.greeting_thanks: A hello, thank you or similar pleasantry.
value_desc.banter_reassurance: Friendly chat or reassurance with no fact in it ("no worries, we've got you").
value_desc.signoff_wrapper: A sign-off, signature block or the lines around one.
value_desc.legal_footer: A confidentiality notice, disclaimer or other legal footer.
value_desc.automated_wrapper: Text a system added around the message: forwarded headers, notification shells, tracking lines.
value_desc.table_scaffolding: A table's empty cells, ruling or repeated headers with no value of their own.
value_desc.section_heading: A heading with no fact of its own and nothing below it to govern.
value_desc.attachment_pointer: A line that only says a file is attached, with no content of its own.
value_desc.speech_filler: Filler words from a call transcript ("um", "yeah, so").
value_desc.page_chrome: Page numbers, running headers, footers and other print furniture.
value_desc.template_instruction: An instruction to whoever fills in a template ("insert site name here").
value_desc.cross_reference: A pointer to another part of the document ("see section 4") with no fact of its own.

reads.label: Why the parser lost the line
reads.values: glued_paragraph | table_cell_glued | table_row_dropped | heading_as_section | checkbox_cell | folded_copy | pasted_quote | split_mid_sentence | spreadsheet_cell | other
reads.desc: Only on a line added by hand (a Missed row, origin labeler): what the parse did that left the line with no atom of its own. It stays on the row as history after a later parse produces the line.

value_desc.glued_paragraph: A fact sentence sat inside a paragraph the parser cut as a whole (a greeting or chatter paragraph), so the fact went with it.
value_desc.table_cell_glued: A table cell's parts ran together, or the cell was read with no atom of its own.
value_desc.table_row_dropped: A table row produced no atom, or only a fragment of one.
value_desc.heading_as_section: A heading was used only as the section path of the lines under it and never became a line.
value_desc.checkbox_cell: A grid's tick-box cell was read as decoration.
value_desc.folded_copy: A dedup fold removed the only copy of the line under its own parent.
value_desc.pasted_quote: A line pasted or quoted from another source was dropped as a repeat, though it was the earliest copy or said something new.
value_desc.split_mid_sentence: A sentence was cut in two, and one half has no atom.
value_desc.spreadsheet_cell: A spreadsheet cell or row produced no atom.
value_desc.other: None of the above; the note says what happened.

reads.label: A real fact later replaced
reads.desc: The fact was true when written and a later line replaced it. Pair it with a contradicts link to the replacement.

reads.label: The text states labor hours
reads.desc: Whether the line itself gives the labor hours. An estimate made by a company rule is not stated.

reads.label: The option is ticked
reads.desc: On a checkbox or option line: whether it was selected. Ticked or not, the line is a fact.

reads.label: What we do with it
reads.desc: What Purtera does with the line. keep: a learned fact Purtera uses, including sites, kept site copies, SOW cover cells and kept risk lines. reject: a real fact Purtera drops on purpose under one of its rules (signature lines, seller promises and status, call scheduling, hardware prices, partner paperwork); it trains the filter. ignore: an excluded input, neither used nor taught as a drop: old hand-built Deal Kit rows and values the parser made up. Noise and background lines (copies, repeats, pointers, summaries) take none.

value_desc.keep: We use the line in our quote or plan.
value_desc.reject: A real fact we drop on purpose under one of our rules; it trains our filter.
value_desc.ignore: We neither use the line nor teach dropping it.

reads.label: Why we reject or ignore it
reads.values: seller_promise | hw_price_not_ours | bom_total_not_ours | quote_reference | vendor_terms | contact_from_crm | handoff_announcement | customer_internal_process | date_only_logistics | superseded | old_manual_deal_kit | out_of_service_line | seller_status_update | partner_internal_process | parser_derived | internal_housekeeping | other
reads.desc: Required when co_action is reject or ignore. The [purtera] part of the note states the rule for this line.

value_desc.seller_promise: The provider's seller promises or offers to act, assures capability, or states pricing posture; sellers own no delivery work, so it plans none.
value_desc.hw_price_not_ours: A hardware price: we do not price hardware we do not sell.
value_desc.bom_total_not_ours: A BOM total or subtotal that is not our price.
value_desc.quote_reference: A reference to a quote number or quote document, not a fact about the work.
value_desc.vendor_terms: A vendor's own terms and conditions.
value_desc.contact_from_crm: A person's contact or email-signature line (name, title, phone, email, address block): the CRM already holds the contact, so the line plans nothing.
value_desc.handoff_announcement: A note that the deal is being handed to another person or team.
value_desc.customer_internal_process: The customer's own internal process, which does not change our work.
value_desc.date_only_logistics: Meeting slots and call scheduling, by either side; a date with no work in it.
value_desc.superseded: Do not use: a replaced value is kept with the superseded reading, never rejected for it.
value_desc.old_manual_deal_kit: A row of an old hand-built Deal Kit; its figures feed only Purtera's own estimate.
value_desc.out_of_service_line: Work in a service line we do not offer.
value_desc.seller_status_update: The provider's seller reports what it did or expects (sent the quote, tried calling) with no fact about the work.
value_desc.partner_internal_process: The partner's own paperwork, approvals or chasing, which do not change the work.
value_desc.parser_derived: A line the parser wrote itself (a count, a disagreement note, an image placeholder), not a line of the deal.
value_desc.internal_housekeeping: Our own bookkeeping, not part of the deal.
value_desc.other: Another Purtera rule, named in the [purtera] line.

reads.label: Our CRM stage, verbatim
reads.desc: The stage exactly as our CRM names it; stage_std is the mapped, universal one.

reads.label: Our crew rule that sets the crew
reads.desc: When one of our crew rules, not the text, sets the crew, e.g. display_over_55in_2_techs.

reads.label: Our labor-hours estimate
reads.desc: Our estimate where the text states no hours (hours_stated=false).

reads.label: How far from our nearest tech base
reads.values: the distance, as written or measured
reads.desc: Travel distance from Purtera's nearest tech base or contractor pool to the site.

reads.label: Our SOW group
reads.desc: The group our own SOW files this line under. The universal kind is scope_facet.

reads.label: Why this SOW group
reads.desc: The reasoning behind scope_category on this line, in a sentence.

reads.label: Which of our delivery fields it fills
reads.desc: The field in our delivery tools this line fills.

reads.label: Where we hold the truth for it
reads.desc: The system we treat as authoritative for this fact, when it is not the document.

reads.label: Whose policy this row carries
reads.desc: Bookkeeping: the company whose co_ keys are on this row. Never a task or an input.

reads.label: How the deal ended
reads.desc: The deal's eventual outcome. Leakage: it is the future, so it is never a parser task or input.

reads.label: The universal type during backfill
reads.desc: Temporary: holds the universal type while a backfill flips policy rejects to it. Never a task.

reads.label: Kept out of training
reads.desc: Bookkeeping: the row is an old manual Deal Kit and never trains a head.

reads.label: Skipped by the labeler
reads.desc: Bookkeeping: the row is set aside (old manual Deal Kit exclusion). Never a task.

reads.label: Who wrote the WHY
reads.desc: Who wrote the WHY in this row's note. person: the labeler wrote it. edited_draft: a model's draft the labeler changed. accepted_draft: a model's draft a person saved as is (one card, or accept-all). machine_draft: a model or deal thread wrote it and no person has saved it since. Set by the page and the accept route on save, and by deal threads on the rows they write.

reads.label: How many visits a site gets
reads.desc: How many separate trips technicians make to one site for this job, as the line states it or as its own words plainly entail: "two visits, install then removal" is 2; a site the line sends technicians back to after the first trip is 2; "3 WLAN visits" at one location is 3. Count trips to the place, not technicians, hours, days on site, devices or sites: "2 techs for 3 days" says nothing about visits unless it says they leave and come back. A line that names a site but never says how often anyone goes there is _absent, and so is a line that is not about visits to a site at all.

reads.label: Why that many visits
reads.desc: The reasoning behind visit_count on this line, in a sentence: which words give the number, or why the line gives none.

reads.label: What work is done at the site
reads.values: install | decommission | replace | relocate | cabling | survey | test | configure | troubleshoot | return_visit
reads.desc: The kind of field work the line says is done at a site, named by the job family it belongs to. A list: a site that gets new equipment and loses the old is install and decommission; a swap of one unit for another in the same place is replace. Read the work the words name, not the equipment brand, the customer's industry or who pays for it. A line that names no work at a site (a contact, a price, a date, an address alone) is _absent.

value_desc.install: New equipment is mounted, connected and brought up where there was none.
value_desc.decommission: Existing equipment is taken out of service and removed, boxed or left for pickup.
value_desc.replace: One unit is swapped for another in the same place: the old one out and the new one in as one piece of work.
value_desc.relocate: Equipment already in place is moved to another spot or another site.
value_desc.cabling: Cable is pulled, terminated, labeled or certified: new runs, drops or patching.
value_desc.survey: The site is walked and documented before any work: measurements, RF readings, photos, an inventory of what is there.
value_desc.test: Something already installed is tested or certified: a circuit, a link, a device's function.
value_desc.configure: Equipment is programmed or set up in software on site, without new hardware work.
value_desc.troubleshoot: A technician is sent to find and fix a fault or to be hands on site for someone remote.
value_desc.return_visit: Technicians go back to the site a second time to finish, remove or check work from the first trip.

reads.label: Why that work
reads.desc: The reasoning behind work_action on this line, in a sentence: which words name the work.

reads.label: What it becomes in the SOW
reads.values: task | customer_responsibility | assumption | exclusion | deliverable | acceptance | fee | site | schedule | overview
reads.desc: What a line written before the statement of work turns into once the provider writes that SOW, judged by what the SOW does with the fact, not by the line's own type or the heading it later sits under. A list: one ask can become a task and an assumption, or an exclusion and a customer responsibility. A customer's standard for how work is done becomes an assumption the price rests on; one entry in a list of drops or devices becomes part of the task that installs them; a request the provider will not take on becomes an exclusion or the customer's own duty. A line the SOW never carries is _absent.

value_desc.task: Work the provider's crew does: a step of the scope or a provider duty.
value_desc.customer_responsibility: Something the customer or its partner must do, supply or decide for the work to go ahead.
value_desc.assumption: A condition the price and plan rest on: access, hours, existing equipment, a standard the work must meet.
value_desc.exclusion: Work or cost the SOW says the job does not include.
value_desc.deliverable: Something handed over at the end: documents, drawings, test results, equipment in place.
value_desc.acceptance: How the work is judged complete: criteria, tests or sign-off.
value_desc.fee: A price, a priced quantity or a billing term in the fees.
value_desc.site: A place where the work happens, listed as a site of the job.
value_desc.schedule: A date, window, duration or order of the work in the timeline.
value_desc.overview: Who the parties are and what the project is, in the introduction.

reads.label: Why it becomes that
reads.desc: The reasoning behind sow_element on this line, in a sentence: what the SOW does with the fact and why.

reads.label: How its words change in the SOW
reads.desc: How the line's fact changes on its way into the statement of work, read against the SOW line it becomes. Set it only where the SOW carries the fact; a line the SOW never carries, or carries with a different number, date or party, is _absent here.

value_desc.verbatim: The SOW carries the line's words as they are, or with only spelling, case or punctuation changed.
value_desc.restated: The SOW says the same single fact in its own words.
value_desc.generalized: A specific entry (one drop, one device, one site's detail) is folded into a broader SOW statement that covers it and others like it.
value_desc.inverted: The SOW turns the ask around: what the customer asked the provider to do becomes an exclusion or the customer's own responsibility.
value_desc.merged: The SOW combines this fact with separate facts from other lines into one statement.

reads.label: Why it changes that way
reads.desc: The reasoning behind sow_transform on this line, in a sentence: how the SOW line's words relate to this line's.

reads.label: Which decision it feeds
reads.values: sites | visits | work_scope | work_quantity | labor_hours | crew | skill_level | work_window | site_access | travel | materials | commercial | schedule | scope_boundary | deliverables | parties | risk_flag
reads.desc: Which decisions of the quote and the statement of work this line is evidence for: the decisions whose answer would change if the line said something different. A list: one line can set the site list and the visits, or the hours and the crew. Judge by what the line's own words let a quoter or SOW writer decide, not by its type, its heading or where it sits in the document: a site list entry that gives a site and its visit count feeds sites and visits; a standard the work must meet feeds work_scope; a line that only greets, thanks or forwards feeds none and is _absent here. Name a decision only when the line states or plainly entails its answer, not when it merely mentions the topic.

value_desc.sites: Which places get work and how many: a site's name, code, address or city on a list of work locations, a stated site count, or a line that adds, drops or closes a location. Not a billing, shipping, vendor or head-office address where no work happens.
value_desc.visits: How many separate trips technicians make to a site: a stated visit count, a return trip to finish or remove work, phases that send the crew back, or a revisit after cutover.
value_desc.work_scope: What field work is done: the tasks, the steps of a method, the equipment installed, removed, moved, tested or configured, and standards the work must meet. This names the tasks and their wording; it is not the count or the time.
value_desc.work_quantity: How much of the work there is: a count of devices, drops, cable runs, ports, rooms, doors or registers, a length of cable or an area in square feet, the number that labor is multiplied by.
value_desc.labor_hours: How long the work takes: hours or minutes per device, per site or per visit, days on site, a productivity rate (square feet per day), or a stated cap on hours.
value_desc.crew: How many technicians work together: a stated headcount, two-person work (lifts, heavy racks, masts), or a request for an extra technician.
value_desc.skill_level: What trade and level the technician needs: a certification, a license, an engineer rather than a technician, a junior or senior level, or a specialty such as RF survey or programming. This sets the rate line.
value_desc.work_window: When work may happen: business hours, after hours, nights, weekends, holidays, a store's closed hours, a maintenance or outage window, a shift cap. This sets the day type, any uplift and the hours assumption.
value_desc.site_access: The physical conditions of getting to the work: ceiling heights, lifts or ladders, escorts, badges, background checks, parking, loading docks, roofs, safety gear, union rules or hazardous materials.
value_desc.travel: Getting technicians to the sites: distance from a technician base, out-of-market or remote sites, mileage, lodging, airfare, per diem or a trip charge.
value_desc.materials: What equipment, cable and material the job needs and who furnishes it: a bill of materials, models and parts, consumables, shipping and receiving of gear, or a line saying the customer or a partner supplies it.
value_desc.commercial: How the job is priced and billed: a price, rate, budget or total, fixed fee versus time and materials, not-to-exceed, purchase order, payment and invoicing terms, a discount, markup or project-management fee.
value_desc.schedule: When the job runs: a start date, a deadline, a duration in weeks or months, the order of phases, a lead time, or a go-live or cutover date.
value_desc.scope_boundary: Who does what: a duty the customer or a partner keeps, work stated as excluded or out of scope, existing conditions the provider does not fix, or work explicitly assigned to the provider against someone else.
value_desc.deliverables: What is handed over and how the work is judged complete: as-built drawings, reports, photos, test or certification results, labels, a punch list, sign-off or acceptance criteria.
value_desc.parties: Who is involved: the end customer, the reseller or partner, the requester, project contacts with their names, emails or phone numbers, the project name.
value_desc.risk_flag: Something open or risky that the quote must flag or assume: an unknown site condition, a quantity or model still to be confirmed, a hazard, a penalty, prevailing wage or certified payroll, insurance or bonding, a permit, or a dependency that could move the price or the plan.

reads.label: Why it feeds that decision
reads.desc: The reasoning behind feeds_decision on this line, in a sentence: which of its words settle which decision, and what the line would have to say to feed a different one or none.

reads.label: When the crew may work
reads.values: business_hours | after_hours | overnight | weekend | holiday | blackout
reads.desc: The time the line says the field work may or must happen, or must avoid. A list: "nights and weekends" is overnight and weekend. Read what the words require of the crew's hours, not who sets them or what they cost: "normal business hours" is business_hours, "after 6 pm" is after_hours, "between 10 pm and 6 am" is overnight, "do not take the system down between 6 and 8 am" is blackout. A line that only states a rate, a deadline date or a duration, with no time of day or day of week for the work, is _absent.

value_desc.business_hours: During ordinary working hours on working days.
value_desc.after_hours: Outside ordinary working hours, in the evening or before opening, on a working day.
value_desc.overnight: Through the night, typically after closing and before opening.
value_desc.blackout: A time when the work must not happen or the system must not be down.

reads.label: Why that window
reads.desc: The reasoning behind work_window on this line, in a sentence: which words give the time, or why there is none.

reads.label: What it takes to reach the work
reads.values: lift | ladder | ground_level | escort | credential | restricted_area
reads.desc: What the crew needs to physically reach the work or get into the place, as the line states it. A list: a ceiling at 35 ft that needs a lift and a badge to enter is lift and credential. ground_level when the line says the work needs no lift or ladder. Read the need, not the price of meeting it or who provides it. A line that names no height, access equipment, escort or entry requirement is _absent.

value_desc.lift: A scissor lift, boom lift or other powered lift is needed to reach the work.
value_desc.ladder: A ladder is enough to reach the work.
value_desc.ground_level: The work is reachable from the floor; no lift or ladder.
value_desc.escort: Someone from the site must accompany the crew.
value_desc.credential: A badge, background check, clearance, safety training or sign-in is needed before entry.
value_desc.restricted_area: The work is in a secured, clean, hazardous or otherwise restricted area with its own rules.

reads.label: Why that access
reads.desc: The reasoning behind access_need on this line, in a sentence: which words give the need, or why there is none.

reads.label: A key detail of the job
reads.desc: Whether the line states one of the few facts that a price and a scope of work for this job must be built on: how many sites, devices, drops or visits; which equipment model; where the work is; when and in what hours it can happen; what access it needs; what the customer supplies; what is left out. true for such a line as the customer or partner gave it. false for a line that is about the job but changes nothing a quote or scope would say (a greeting, a status update, a reason, a repeat, a general remark), even when it is a real fact.

reads.label: Why it is or is not a key detail
reads.desc: The reasoning behind job_detail on this line, in a sentence: which fact the price or scope rests on, or why none.

reads.label: How long the cable runs are
reads.desc: The length of a cable run the line states, in feet (convert metres): "each AP run will not exceed approximately 150 feet" is 150; "runs of 15 to 25 feet" is 25, the longest. A total of all cable installed, a ceiling height, a distance between sites or a spool length is not a run length. A line that gives no run length is _absent.

reads.label: Why that run length
reads.desc: The reasoning behind run_length on this line, in a sentence: which words give the length, or why there is none.

reads.label: What kind of price
reads.desc: The basis of a price or estimate the line states or asks for: whether it is a rough number, a price the provider stands behind, a cap, a set of rates the total will come from, or the customer's own budget. Read what the words commit to, not the amount. A line that states no price, estimate or budget is _absent.

value_desc.rom_estimate: A rough, budgetary or ballpark number that will change once the job is surveyed or defined.
value_desc.firm_price: A fixed price for the stated scope, whatever the hours turn out to be.
value_desc.not_to_exceed: A ceiling the total may not pass, billed up to it.
value_desc.rate_based: Rates per hour, day, unit or site, so the total follows the work actually done.
value_desc.customer_budget: What the customer has to spend or expects to pay, not the provider's price.

reads.label: Why that price basis
reads.desc: The reasoning behind price_basis on this line, in a sentence: which words set the basis, or why there is none.

reads.label: What part the person plays in the job
reads.values: requester | decision_maker | onsite_contact | project_manager | technical_contact | billing_contact | end_customer | reseller
reads.desc: The role in this job the line gives a person or company. A list: "Jo, the store manager, will meet the tech and sign off" is onsite_contact and decision_maker. Read the role the words give, never a title alone: a signature that names a title but no part in the job is _absent. A line that names no person or company with a part in the job is _absent.

value_desc.requester: Asks for the work or the quote.
value_desc.decision_maker: Approves the price, the scope or the sign-off.
value_desc.onsite_contact: Meets the crew, gives access or answers questions at the site.
value_desc.project_manager: Runs the schedule and coordination of the job.
value_desc.technical_contact: Answers technical questions: network, configuration, equipment.
value_desc.billing_contact: Receives invoices or handles purchase orders and payment.
value_desc.end_customer: The company the work is ultimately for, when another company buys it.
value_desc.reseller: The company that buys the work to resell it to the end customer.

reads.label: Why that role
reads.desc: The reasoning behind party_role on this line, in a sentence: which words give the person their part, or why there is none.

relations_doc: How one atom stands to another. lead_in already ties a list item to its header; these are the links a person draws.

relations.label: Announces / scopes the atoms below
relations.desc: From the line that opens a block to every atom it covers. Carries no text of its own.

relations.label: Backs it up
relations.desc: From a line to an earlier line that backs it up with evidence or detail: a count supports the total it adds to.

relations.label: Answers the question
relations.desc: From an answer to the question it settles. A question with no answer stays open.

relations.label: Says the opposite
relations.desc: Two lines that cannot both hold for one fact. A replaced value points at the line that changed it and at the new value's line; two live opposing values, and changed cells across drafts, point at each other. A request the statement of work refuses points at the line that says no.

relations.label: The same fact, said twice
relations.desc: From a copy to the learned line it repeats: the same fact said again, word for word or reworded, in a quoted email, a forward, an older draft or a summary. It points one way, at the earliest original by its own date; an older statement-of-work draft points at the signed or latest draft instead. The copy is background, not an input. The same words under a different parent that changes who owes it, when, where or the price are not a copy. Unlike supports (adds evidence), context (helps read it) or near_miss (looks alike, answers differently).

relations.label: Background for it
relations.desc: From a line to an earlier one that is background needed to read it, without backing it up or contradicting it.

relations.label: Cannot happen until that one does
relations.desc: From a task or commitment to the dependency it waits on: "we will coordinate a date" is blocked_by "TVs are with the shipping carrier".

relations.label: That event starts it
relations.desc: From a triggered task to the line saying its event happened: "we will coordinate a date" is triggered_by "TVs were delivered today".

relations.label: Worked out from it
relations.desc: From a statement-of-work line to the one earliest line that first asked for or offered its fact (the request bullet, the customer's email), never to a copy of it; or from a value worked out to the lines it was worked out from. Every other restatement is context or supports.

relations.label: Looks alike, answers differently
relations.desc: Two lines that look or sound alike but answer differently, such as the same wording about a different party, site or item. The WHY of each says what makes the difference.

asks_supplier_doc: Does 'who supplies or does it?' have an answer for this type? The card showed that question on EVERY type, so three quarters of the time it invited an answer to a question the sentence does not ask -- and a head trained on those learns the axes are independent noise. Declared here rather than guessed from the type's name.
